question: Can a notwithstanding-clause declaration remain in force indefinitely without renewal?
generated_answer:
A great question about Canadian constitutional law!

In Canada, the notwithstanding clause, also known as Section 33 of the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, allows a province or the federal government to override certain provisions of the Charter for a period of five years. This clause is often used to enact legislation that may infringe on individual rights or freedoms, but is deemed necessary for a particular purpose.

According to Section 33, a declaration made under the notwithstanding clause "shall cease to have effect five years after it comes into force or on such earlier date as may be specified in the declaration." This means that a notwithstanding-clause declaration is not indefinite and will automatically expire after five years, unless it is renewed or a specific earlier date is specified.

To remain in force beyond the initial five-year period, the government must re-enact the legislation and re-declare the use of the notwithstanding clause. This requires a new vote in the legislature and a new proclamation, which can be subject to political and public scrutiny.

In summary, a notwithstanding-clause declaration cannot remain in force indefinitely without renewal. It is subject to a five-year sunset clause, after which it must be re-enacted and re-declared to continue in effect.
